entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Tatian, an Assyrian Christian apologist and theologian of the 2nd century (c. 120 – c. 173 CE), was a pivotal, yet controversial, figure in early Christian thought, best known for his *Diatessaron*, the first harmonized gospel, and his radical asceticism. His intellectual journey took him from Syria to Rome, where he studied philosophy before converting to Christianity, ultimately establishing a distinctive, often heterodox, theological school. His work reflects the intense intellectual ferment and syncretism of the Roman Imperial period, engaging directly with Greek philosophy while advocating for a distinctively Christian worldview.

Tatian's most enduring contribution was the *Diatessaron*, a single continuous narrative woven from the four canonical gospels—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—completed around 170 CE. This innovative text became the standard gospel harmony for Syriac-speaking Christianity for centuries, effectively replacing the individual gospels in many regions until the 5th century. Beyond the *Diatessaron*, Tatian authored the *Oratio ad Graecos* (Address to the Greeks), an apologetic work fiercely critiquing Greek culture and philosophy while defending the antiquity and moral superiority of Christian doctrine. His later years saw him embrace extreme asceticism, including strict vegetarianism, lifelong celibacy, and rejection of wine, leading to his association with the Encratite movement.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tatian's *Diatessaron* revolutionized biblical study and liturgical practice in Syriac Christianity for over two centuries, impacting figures like Ephrem the Syrian. His apologetic works also critically engaged with Greek philosophy, shaping early Christian intellectual defense.
